The AI industry just crossed a financial Rubicon.

Anthropic filed its S-1 this week, setting up what could be one of the largest tech IPOs in history. On the same day, Meta moved to raise up to $95 billion for AI infrastructure.

This is not just big money. This is a structural shift in how AI gets built, funded, and governed.

When an AI company goes public, it opens its books. Unit economics. Safety spending. Governance frameworks. Revenue concentration. All of it becomes visible — not just to investors, but to every enterprise customer evaluating whether to build on that platform for the next five years.

For business leaders, the signal is unmistakable: AI vendor selection is now a financial due diligence exercise, not just a technical evaluation. The providers that survive public-market scrutiny will set the standard. The rest will consolidate or disappear.

The question is not whether your organization uses AI. It is whether the AI you depend on will still be standing — and still be trustworthy — in three years.
